_note: Wooden farm tools: hoes, spades, rakes and forks cut and shaped from seasoned timber. The tool a farm worker draws when iron tools are short (data/world/trades.json tool_basket order). The hours factor against iron is sourced in data/world/trades.json (Semyonov 1974 via Shukurov et al.); wood per tonne and carpenter hours are derived below from a timed, dimensioned hand-carved paddle (Complaint 650).

wooden_tools_kg.basis: per tonne of finished wooden farm tools (hoes, spades, rakes, forks, sickle handles), counted by the mass of the tools
wooden_tools_kg.yield_basis: DERIVED from a comparable carved object (conf C: ballpark; a paddle stands in for a spade). Duckworks Magazine, making a Greenland paddle (https://duckworksmagazine.com/15/howto/greenland/, opened): "spend 10 to 14 hours making each paddle"; a 2x6 board; paddle 91 inches long, blade 3 to 3.25 inches wide, loom 19 inches long and 1.25 by 1.5 inch oval. VOLUME: loom 19 x (pi/4 x 1.25 x 1.5 = 1.47) = 28 cubic inches; two blades about 36 x 3.25 x 0.5 = 58 each, so about 145 cubic inches finished; the blank is a 2x6 of 1.5 x 5.5 x 91 = 751 cubic inches (nominal sizes; blank thickness and blade thickness are my approximations). Finished share 145 / 751 = 0.19, so 1000 kg of tools needs about 1000 / 0.19 = 5200 kg of seasoned timber (hewn waste 81 percent). MASS: ash is the traditional wood for tool handles, density 710 kg/m3 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fraxinus_excelsior, opened); 145 cubic inches = 2.4 litres = 1.7 kg. HOURS: 10 hours (the low end, since a farm tool needs no sanding or gluing) / 1.7 kg = 5.9 hours a kilogram, taken as 6000 hours a tonne. Ceilings: the paddle's hours include laminating and sanding to a fine grit, and power planing; a farm tool is cruder. Needs no technology.
